results.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
results.proof_sketch: The sparse bound is at most n√m exactly when m^(4/3)≤n√m, equivalently m^(5/6)≤n, or m≤n^(6/5). The dense bound n² is at most a polylogarithmic multiple of n√m when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n. Writing m=n^a, the two bounds cross when 4a/3=2, namely a=3/2. Before that point the ratio exponent is 5a/6−1; afterward it is 1−a/2. Both equal 1/4 at a=3/2, the maximum.

results.claim: Balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, either the insertion closes a cycle, or one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, and the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological. In the latter case, all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
results.proof_sketch: If v already reaches u, report that path together with u→v; no balanced cut is asserted. Otherwise, within [v,u], let D be the inclusive descendants of v and C the inclusive ancestors of u. They are disjoint, since a common vertex would give v→u. Sweep a positional cut from before v to after u and set Δ=|D on the left|−|C on the right|. Initially Δ<0, finally Δ>0, and crossing a vertex of D or C raises Δ by exactly one. Thus some cut between v and u has Δ=0; take F=D∩L and B=C∩R. Then v∈F, u∈B. In the stable block order, an old edge F→(L\F) contradicts descendant closure, an edge (R\B)→B contradicts ancestor closure, and an edge F→B would give an old v-to-u path. Every other reversed direction is forbidden by the old topological order. The new edge u→v points from B to F. Finally, each b∈B reaches each f∈F through b→…→u→v→…→f, while previously b lay after f and hence could not reach it.

results.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
results.proof_sketch: For non-cycle violating update i, write |B_i|=|F_i|=q_i. Its q_i² pairs are newly reachable, and reachability is monotone, so these pairs are disjoint between updates and Σq_i²≤n(n−1). With at most m such updates, Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σq_i≤√(mΣq_i²)=O(n√m). Min/max heaps enumerate the two searches in topological order; non-root heap insertions and stale entries are charged to scanned adjacency entries, while selected-vertex heap work is Õ(Σq_i). A balanced sequence tree performs stable extraction and reinsertion in Õ(q_i). Edge storage and root setup cost Õ(m). If processing stops at the first cycle, that final search adds at most Õ(n) selected-vertex work plus its contribution to A. Hence the total is Õ(m+n√m+A). Under the stated directional-degree condition, A=Õ(Σq_i+n). For distinct simple edges, m≤n² implies m≤n√m, so the conditional bound is Õ(n√m).

results.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
results.proof_sketch: Use initial order v,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r. First insert v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z for every i,j, giving 3r order-consistent edges. Then insert u_i→v for i=1,…,r. Immediately before update i, the maintained order is u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,u_i,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r, so the balanced sets are F={v}, B={u_i}. Vertex u_i already reaches z and every w_j, and it has no proper ancestor; therefore only (u_i,v) becomes newly reachable. Nevertheless, v retains all r outgoing entries v→w_j, so expanding v by a full-list scan costs r on each of r updates. The sequence has r additional edges, hence m=4r, and incurs exactly r² scans. This refutes only the automatic scan charging, not the possibility of a more selective adjacency mechanism.

results.claim: Interval-pruning lemma: in a compatible-search round whose current forward-minimum and backward-maximum candidates are f≺b, forward expansion may ignore out-neighbors right of b and backward expansion may ignore in-neighbors left of f. The pruned search still detects every cycle-forming insertion and, in the non-cycle branch, selects the same first q descendants and last q ancestors that yield a balanced cut.
results.proof_sketch: Forward candidates move only right and backward candidates only left, so a discarded vertex outside the opposing frontier can never later be selected in a compatible round. This preserves the selected prefixes and suffixes in the non-cycle branch. For cycle detection, fix an old path v=p₀→…→p_k=u. Suppose expansion of a forward-reached p_i first tries to discard p_(i+1) because it is right of b. Every path vertex from p_(i+1) through u is then right of b. Starting at u, backward induction shows that each has already been backward-expanded: when its successor was expanded, its predecessor was right of the then-current forward frontier and hence was not pruned. In particular, backward expansion of p_(i+1) marked p_i, intersecting the forward reached set—a contradiction. Therefore forward reach advances along the path until the reached sets intersect. The symmetric pruning is used in that backward induction. Thus the search cannot stop acyclically when v reaches u.

results.claim: Selective-expansion refinement: let H sum, over all compatible-search expansions, min{outdeg(f),|{x:f≺x≼b}|} on the forward side and min{indeg(b),|{x:f≼x≺b}|} on the backward side. There is an explicit combinatorial implementation with total update time Õ(m+n√m+H). Moreover H≤A, and H=O(m) on the rescanning family of the preceding audited claim.
results.proof_sketch: Track degrees, store edges in a deterministic dictionary keyed by immutable vertex identifiers, and retain the balanced sequence tree for the topological order. To expand f, either scan its whole outgoing list and retain heads through b, or enumerate (f,b] and test f→x in the dictionary, choosing the smaller count. Expand b symmetrically using its incoming list or [f,b). The interval-pruning lemma proves correctness. Rank, interval-enumeration, dictionary, and heap overheads are polylogarithmic; every probe and every generated heap entry is charged to H. Replacing A by H in the audited accounting gives Õ(m+n√m+H). Each minimum is at most the corresponding fully scanned degree, so H≤A. In the preceding family f=v and b=u_i are adjacent on every violating update, giving H=O(r)=O(m), even though A=r².

results.claim: The selective parameter H is still not bounded by Õ(n√m): there is a DAG sequence with n=3r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, but both the forward degree and active forward interval have size at least r, giving H=r².
results.proof_sketch: Start in order v,x₁,…,x_r,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r. Insert v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z for all i,j, then insert u_i→v in increasing i. Before update i the order is u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,x₁,…,x_r,u_i,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r. Thus F={v}, B={u_i}, and only (u_i,v) is newly reachable because u_i already reaches z and every w_j. Forward vertex v has r outgoing edges, while (v,u_i] contains r+1 vertices, so its selective cost is exactly r on every update; the backward cost is zero. Hence H=r². Since n√m=(3r+2)·2√r=Θ(r^(3/2)), the ratio is Θ(√r), not polylogarithmic.

results.claim: Padding sharpens the selective-expansion obstruction across every subquadratic density: for integers r≥1 and 0≤s≤r, adjoining a disconnected s-vertex transitive DAG to the preceding sequence gives n=3r+s+2, m=4r+binom(s,2), while every violating update still has q=1, creates one new reachability pair, and contributes total H=r². Consequently H/(n√m)=Θ(r/√(r+s²)). For every fixed a∈[1,2), choosing s=⌈r^(a/2)⌉ gives m=Θ(n^a) and a polynomial gap Θ(n^(1−a/2)); at a=3/2 the gap is Θ(n^(1/4)), whereas at the quadratic or polylogarithmically near-quadratic boundary it is only constant or polylogarithmic.
results.proof_sketch: Place new vertices y₁,…,y_s after all w_j and insert every edge y_j→y_k with j<k before the violating updates. These edges are order-consistent and the y-component is disconnected from the original vertices, so it never participates in a compatible search and changes neither the maintained-order invariant nor any reachability delta of the original sequence. Thus the preceding q=1, singleton-fresh-pair, and per-update H=r conclusions remain exact, while the vertex and final-edge counts gain s and binom(s,2). Since s≤r, n=Θ(r), m=Θ(r+s²), and the displayed ratio follows. Taking s=⌈r^(a/2)⌉ gives the fixed-density statement. At the exact crossover, r=t⁴ and s=t³ yield n=Θ(t⁴), m=Θ(t⁶)=Θ(n^(3/2)), H=t⁸=Θ(n²), and gap Θ(t)=Θ(n^(1/4)). If s=r/log^C r, the ratio is Θ(log^C r), and if s=Θ(r) it is Θ(1), identifying the dense boundary. This is a limitation of the stated selective implementation and its H-charge, not a lower bound against all combinatorial algorithms.

final_writeup:
This revision remains PARTIAL: it strengthens the obstruction to the audited balanced-cut implementation but does not give the requested unconditional Õ(n√m) algorithm.

The two source-stated bounds give Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}), meeting the target for m≤n^(6/5) and for m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n, with worst gap Õ(n^(1/4)) at m=Θ(n^(3/2)).

For a violating insertion u→v, report a cycle if v already reaches u. Otherwise, sweep a cut across [v,u]. Inclusive descendants D of v and ancestors C of u are disjoint, and |D on the left|−|C on the right| rises in unit steps from negative to positive, so it is zero at some cut. With F the descendants on the left and B the ancestors on the right, |F|=|B| and the stable order

(L\F), B, F, (R\B)

is topological. Descendant closure, ancestor closure, the old topological order, and the absence of a v-to-u path exclude every possible backward old edge; u→v runs from B to F. Every pair in B×F becomes newly reachable. Thus, writing q_i=|B_i|=|F_i|, monotonicity gives Σq_i²≤n(n−1), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σq_i=O(n√m).

The heap-and-sequence-tree implementation costs Õ(m+n√m+A), where A counts full directional adjacency-list scans. The n=2r+2 family shows A can be r² even though all r violations have q=1 and create one new pair each.

Interval pruning permits a more selective implementation. In a compatible round with minimum forward candidate f and maximum backward candidate b, expand f by the cheaper of scanning its outgoing list and enumerating (f,b] with edge-dictionary tests; expand b symmetrically. Monotone opposing frontiers preserve the balanced sets, and a path induction shows that pruning cannot hide a cycle. If H sums these per-expansion minima, the resulting time is Õ(m+n√m+H), with H≤A. This eliminates the first rescanning example.

The neutral-interval family defeats this refinement: begin in order v,x₁,…,x_r,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r, insert v→w_j, z→w_j, u_i→z, and then insert u_i→v in increasing i. Each violation still has F={v}, B={u_i}, and only (u_i,v) newly reachable. But outdeg(v)=r and (v,u_i] has r+1 vertices, so H=r².

This obstruction is not confined to the sparse range where the source’s m^(4/3) algorithm already suffices. Append s≤r vertices y₁,…,y_s after the construction and insert the disconnected transitive DAG containing every y_j→y_k for j<k. These order-consistent edges do not affect any search or reachability delta. The resulting sequence has n=3r+s+2, m=4r+binom(s,2), and H=r², so H/(n√m)=Θ(r/√(r+s²)). In particular, taking r=t⁴ and s=t³ gives m=Θ(n^(3/2)) and an Θ(n^(1/4)) gap, exactly at the crossover where the source-stated guarantees are furthest from the target. More generally, every fixed density m=Θ(n^a), 1≤a<2, admits a polynomial H-gap Θ(n^(1−a/2)); the gap becomes only polylogarithmic when m is within polylogarithmic factors of n² and constant at quadratic density.

This is an obstruction to the direct list-versus-interval implementation, not a lower bound for every combinatorial algorithm. The unrestricted intermediate-density target remains unresolved. This route would require a reusable dynamic subset-successor mechanism, or a different global invariant, whose maintenance and invalidations avoid paying again for the same negative adjacency information.
